examples.problem_statement: What is the sum of the numbers in the grid below?

solution.result: the leading positive and negative terms of row 1 cancel to 0
solution.description: Look across the first row and pair each negative term with its positive twin; each pair sums to zero, so those columns add nothing.
Add only the terms of row 1 that survived the cancellation, which sit in the two far-right columns.

solution.operation: \text{grid sum} = \text{sum of the two far-right columns}
solution.result: the problem reduces to summing six row-pairs
solution.description: Apply the same cancellation to every other row, since each row repeats the pattern; only the two far-right columns ever contribute.
Compute the far-right-column total for each row in turn, from the first row down to the final row.
Add the six surviving row totals together to get the sum of the whole grid.

key_reminders: A term and its negative cancel to zero, so those columns can be dropped before adding anything.
When every row repeats the same cancellation pattern, the grid sum collapses to the sum of the surviving columns.
common_mistakes: Adding all of the grid's entries one by one instead of noticing the cancelling pairs in each row.
Cancelling the pairs but then forgetting to carry the same reduction through the remaining rows.

examples.problem_statement: Quantity A: The combined area of four circles, each with radius 1. Quantity B: The area of a circle with radius 2. Compare the two quantities.

solution.description: Start with Quantity A and find the area of just one of its circles by putting radius 1 into the circle-area formula.
Multiply that single-circle area by four, since Quantity A asks for the combined area of four identical circles.
Turn to Quantity B and use its radius of 2 in the same area formula.

solution.result: the two quantities are always equal
solution.description: Set the two computed quantities side by side and see that they match exactly, which selects the 'equal' answer choice.

key_reminders: The area of a circle is \pi r^2, so radius enters squared, not linearly.
For a combined area, compute one shape's area first and then multiply by the count.
common_mistakes: Assuming doubling the radius from 1 to 2 doubles the area, which would make Quantity B only 2\pi instead of 4\pi.
Comparing radii or circumferences (four circles of radius 1 versus one of radius 2) rather than the areas actually asked for.

concept.sub_category: Reading Comprehension - function of a sentence

examples.problem_statement: For each of Questions 1 to 9, select one answer choice unless otherwise instructed. Which of the following best describes the function of the second sentence (“A Dream … essayists”) in the context of the passage as a whole?

solution.operation: Read the second sentence against the passage's overall description and name what it does there.
solution.result: the sentence describes what is appealing about the collection in the context of the author's childhood tastes
solution.description: Fix the sentence's job in the passage before touching the choices, since the question asks for function rather than content.

solution.operation: Test Choice A: does the sentence give examples, and does the collection show awareness of the tenuous nature of representations of reality?
solution.description: Reject A because the sentence provides no examples and the collection is never credited with that awareness.

solution.operation: Test Choice C: does the passage discuss adult enjoyment being more sophisticated than childhood enjoyment?
solution.description: Reject C because the passage contains no discussion or even suggestion of a more sophisticated adult basis for enjoyment, however plausible that idea sounds on its own.

solution.operation: Test Choice D: does the sentence present inadequacies of the collection?
solution.description: Reject D because this sentence describes the collection's virtues; the aspects the author finds inadequate are not addressed until later in the passage.

solution.operation: Test Choice E: does the passage treat the collection's variety as a hindrance to contextualization?
solution.description: Reject E because the passage says the variety is what makes the collection a rich read, with no suggestion that it hinders contextualization.

solution.operation: Match the function identified in step 1 to the surviving choice.
solution.description: Confirm B, which states that the sentence elaborates on how the collection fulfills the author's childhood criteria for a pleasurable book.

examples.answer: Choice B: To elaborate on how A Dream fulfills the author’s childhood criteria for a pleasurable book

key_reminders: A function question asks what a sentence does in the passage, not merely what it says.
A wrong choice can be true of the world and still be unsupported by the passage.
Locate where in the passage a claim appears; material introduced later cannot be the function of this sentence.
common_mistakes: Choosing C because the sophistication contrast feels reasonable, even though the passage never raises it.
Choosing D by importing the author's later criticisms into a sentence that is describing virtues.
Choosing E by reading the collection's variety as a flaw when the passage calls it a source of richness.
